Baby & Child

How to explain death as children grow

Updated: November 16, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

On Saturday, a child puts out one extra cup for the grandfather who used to come for breakfast. Last night they heard that he had died. Today they are trying to work out whether that changes Saturday, too. Start with the question in front of you. There will be other chances to talk.

Use words your child can return to

Tell them plainly who died. You could say, “Grandad died yesterday. His body stopped working. He cannot breathe or feel pain. He cannot come back for breakfast.” Say a little, then pause. If you know how he died, offer a brief, accurate explanation. If you are still waiting to learn why, you can tell the child that.

Children piece together several ideas. Death lasts forever. The body’s functions have ended. All living things eventually die. There is a physical cause, even when adults do not yet know what it was. You can answer one question at a time. Saying someone has gone to sleep or gone away can leave a young child afraid of bedtime or waiting by the door.

Babies and toddlers notice who is missing

A baby may reach for someone who usually lifts them out of their cot. A toddler may watch the door or become clingy when a familiar caregiver cries or leaves. A steady voice, a familiar lap and the usual snack or bedtime song can help a child feel cared for through changes they cannot yet explain.

Name the person and keep your explanation short. When a toddler asks again, the same words are fine. Tell them who is here now and who will look after them next. If you are grieving too, ask someone your child knows to take on a familiar part of the day.

Preschoolers and early school years bring new questions

A child may know that Grandpa cannot eat breakfast and still ask whether he can come back for their birthday. Ask what they think has happened. Their answer can reveal the piece they are working on. They may return to a game as soon as you answer and bring up a different question tomorrow.

In a British interview study of children aged four to eleven and adults, some children understood parts of the concept by age four or five. Older children tended to explain the causes of death in more biological terms. These were patterns in one sample. Your child’s own question is a better guide to the next sentence than their birthday.

When a school-age child asks if it was their fault

A child who argued with Grandad the day before he died may remember every word. Ask what makes them wonder about the argument. Tell them directly, “Being cross with Grandad did not make him die.” If there was a serious illness, explain it in a few words. Explain that ordinary illnesses such as a cold usually get better.

They may ask whether you will die, too. Give an honest answer and bring it back to the worry you can address today. You might say, “Everyone dies at some point. I expect to be here to care for you for a long time. Auntie is picking you up after school today.” If you yourself are seriously ill, tell the child what you know and which adults are making plans for their care.

Let teenagers choose how to talk

A teenager may understand what happened and still want to know how a person can be at breakfast one week and gone the next. Give them chances to ask for more detail. A conversation in the car or over a shared chore may feel easier than sitting down for a family discussion. Ask which details they want a teacher or friend to know.

Time with friends, music, drawing or keeping a photograph can all have a place. Let them see how you remember the person, without making them responsible for comforting you. If they brush off an invitation to talk, offer another quiet opportunity later.

Notice when grief is getting in the way

Sadness can sit alongside play and laughter. Some children need more help with familiar tasks, wake at night, have stomach aches or find it hard to concentrate at school. Ask how they are managing and check in with the adults who see them during the day. An anniversary or another change can bring up new questions.

Contact the child’s healthcare professional or a bereavement support service if you are worried, especially with persistent withdrawal, loss of sleep, difficulty attending school or risky behaviour. Take any statement about wanting to die seriously and seek urgent professional help. If the child might act soon or you cannot keep them safe, stay with them and contact local emergency services.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Use plain words and ask what the child has understood.

Explain the change in everyday care and correct beliefs that the child caused the death.

Look for distress that interferes with daily life and act urgently on immediate safety concerns.

How BeMama can help

BeMama follows the example of a missing place at breakfast to show how an ordinary family routine can bring up different questions as a child grows.

When to seek help

Seek urgent professional help if a child says they want to die. Stay with them and contact local emergency services if they may act soon or you cannot keep them safe.

Evidence notes updated: November 16, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Say who died and explain simply that their body has stopped working and they cannot return.
  • Tell a young child who will collect them, feed them and put them to bed today.
  • Ask what the child thinks caused the death and address any misplaced guilt directly.
  • Give a teenager choices about when to talk and whom they want involved.

Frequently asked questions

Do babies or toddlers understand a death?

They may notice an absence, a break in routine or a caregiver’s distress before they can understand death in words. Offer closeness, predictable care and a short, consistent explanation as their questions emerge.

What can I tell a six-year-old who keeps asking when someone will return?

Use the word “died” and explain again that the person cannot come back. Ask what they miss about the visit. You can make room for both the fact of the death and a memory, such as making the breakfast the person used to cook.

How much detail does a school-age child need?

Ask what they already know, correct misunderstandings and give a truthful answer to their particular question. Make it clear that a thought, wish or argument did not cause the death. You can revisit the subject if they want more information later.

What if my teenager would rather talk to someone else?

Ask who feels comfortable to speak with and help them make contact. Let them know you are available and keep checking how they are managing. Serious distress, withdrawal or concerns about safety deserve professional support.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
